RQ1: How has marginal price formation in the GB Balancing Mechanism evolved between 2023 and 2025, and how does this differ by technology, bid/offer side and system condition?

Study window: 1 January 2023–31 December 2025 · Generated: 2026-07-17 11:13

Figure 1. Technology composition of attributed marginality by active side

Figure 1. Tie-adjusted share of attributed marginal Settlement Period weight within bid-active and offer-active periods, 2023–2025. Each Settlement Period contributes a total weight of one across co-marginal BMUs. Technologies are ordered by their combined share, with a common colour used for each technology across both sides. The ten largest technologies by combined bid- and offer-side share are shown; “Other” is the original BM technology classification rather than an aggregation of omitted categories.

What the figure measures

The figure compares the technology composition of the margin under the two system conditions that activate different sides of the Balancing Mechanism. Bid-active periods correspond to a long system (NIV < 0), while offer-active periods correspond to a short system (NIV > 0). Shares are normalised separately within each side, allowing their technology mixes to be compared even though the numbers of bid- and offer-active periods differ.

Main result. The most represented technologies on the bid side are CCGT (44%), Battery (17%), and Wind (12%). On the offer side they are CCGT (46%), Pumped storage (18%), and Battery (17%). CCGT accounts for 43.8% of bid-active and 46.1% of offer-active marginal-setting weight; batteries account for 16.8% and 17.3%, respectively.

Interpretation

The two halves do not mirror one another. Among technologies accounting for at least 1% across the two sides, Pumped storage has the strongest offer orientation (12.6 percentage points more on the offer side), while Wind has the strongest bid orientation (12.0 percentage points more on the bid side). Pumped storage is strongly offer-oriented, whereas wind and biomass are bid-oriented; biomass represents 6.1% of bid-active weight but only 1.3% of offer-active weight. This is evidence that marginal price formation is technologically asymmetric across system conditions: different balancing resources occupy the margin when the system needs downward rather than upward adjustment. The comparison therefore supports analysing bid- and offer-active periods separately rather than treating the GB Balancing Mechanism as a single homogeneous marginal market.

The main-text figure retains the ten technologies needed to show the substantive composition and asymmetry clearly. Remaining technologies each accounted for less than 1% of marginal weight on both sides. They are reported individually in Appendix A rather than combined into an additional “Other” category; “Other” in the figure is an existing technology classification.

Method and limitations

Each settlement period contributes one unit of marginal-setting weight. Where multiple BMUs share the marginal price, that unit is divided equally among the co-marginal BMUs before aggregation to technology. This prevents periods with more candidate rows from receiving greater influence. The analysis covers 50,684 settlement periods: approximately 26,987 bid-active and 23,697 offer-active periods.

The chart measures representation at the identified margin, not causal price impact, bidding conduct, market power, or generating capacity. A technology can appear frequently at the margin without producing the largest variation in System Price. Those questions require the conditional-price and RF/SHAP evidence presented in later RQ1 figures.

Figure 2. System Price distributions by marginal technology and active side

Figure 2. System Price distributions by attributed marginal technology and active side. Thick intervals show the interquartile range and open circles show the median. Thin extensions show the directionally relevant price tails: P10 and P5 for bid-active periods, and P90 and P95 for offer-active periods. Technologies are shown in the same order across both panels. Each distribution contains one observation per Settlement Period–technology combination, preventing multiple co-marginal BMUs of the same technology from duplicating System Price.

What the figure measures

Figure 1 established how often technologies were represented at the margin. Figure 2 instead asks what System Price looked like when each technology was marginal. The sided tail definition follows the economic direction of balancing: unusually low prices are relevant when the system is long and bids are active, whereas unusually high prices are relevant when the system is short and offers are active.

Main result. Offer-active conditional medians are consistently above their bid-active counterparts. CCGT and battery central prices are comparatively close within each side: their bid-active medians are £62.5/MWh and £59.0/MWh, while their offer-active medians are £113.9/MWh and £107.2/MWh. The larger technological separation occurs in the directional tails: pumped storage reaches an offer-side P95 of £203.0/MWh, while wind reaches a bid-side P5 of −£61.6/MWh.

Interpretation

The shared CCGT–battery core in Figure 1 does not imply identical price consequences. Their central conditional distributions overlap substantially, but technologies separate more clearly in the tails. Pumped storage is associated with the upper offer-side tail, while wind is associated with the lowest bid-side prices. This distinction prevents marginal frequency from being treated as synonymous with price impact: a technology can appear frequently at the margin without being associated with especially extreme outcomes, and a less frequent technology can be disproportionately visible in a directional price tail.

Method and limitations

Several co-marginal BMUs of the same technology do not replicate the same System Price: the calculation retains one observation for each Settlement Period × technology × active-side combination. If different technologies are co-marginal in the same Settlement Period, that observed price contributes once to each applicable technology distribution. The intervals are descriptive conditional distributions, not causal estimates of a technology's effect on price, bidding conduct, or market power.

Figure 3. Quarterly technology trajectories by active side

Figure 3. Quarterly evolution of attributed marginality among the principal changing technologies. Lines show tie-adjusted shares within bid-active and offer-active Settlement Periods. The bid-active panel presents CCGT, battery and wind; the offer-active panel presents CCGT, battery and pumped storage. Technologies use the same colours as Figures 1 and 2, and both panels use a common vertical scale. Quarterly samples ranged from 2,066 to 2,434 bid-active periods and from 1,825 to 2,196 offer-active periods.

What the figure measures

The trajectories reveal changes hidden by the pooled result in Figure 1. Shares are normalised separately within each side and quarter, so they describe composition rather than the absolute number of long- or short-system periods. The focused design foregrounds the technologies central to each side's transition while the quarterly sample-size ranges provide denominator context.

Main result. Battery representation increased on both sides: from 3.2% to 26.9% of offer-active marginal weight and from 0.8% to 36.2% on the bid side. Over the same quarters, CCGT changed from 53.0% to 45.0% on offers and from 54.8% to 33.6% on bids. Battery first exceeded CCGT on the bid side in 2025 Q3 and remained ahead in Q4. Pumped storage's offer share moved from 33.3% to 10.4%, while wind's bid share moved from 15.9% to 5.6%.

Interpretation

The pooled market has a stable-looking CCGT–battery core, but the quarterly trajectories show that this composition was not stationary. Battery marginality expanded progressively rather than appearing as a one-off step change. The technologies moving alongside that growth differed by side: pumped storage is the key offer-side comparator, while wind is the key bid-side comparator. This side-specific view therefore addresses how marginal price formation evolved, rather than reporting only the endpoint or pooled average.

Method and limitations

Quarterly shares use the same tie adjustment as Figure 1: one unit per Settlement Period divided equally among co-marginal BMUs, then aggregated to technology. A quarterly share can change because a technology's attributed marginal weight changed, because competing technologies changed, or both. The trajectories are descriptive and should not be interpreted as causal displacement without the accompanying battery and unit-level evidence.

Figure 4. Directional extreme-price representation relative to overall marginality

Figure 4. Directional extreme-price representation relative to overall marginality. Bars show each technology's share of tie-adjusted marginal weight in the directionally relevant System Price tail minus its overall share within the corresponding active side. Positive values indicate overrepresentation in extreme-price periods, while negative values indicate underrepresentation. The bid-active tail comprises the lowest 5% of bid-active System Prices, at or below −£17.98/MWh; the offer-active tail comprises the highest 5% of offer-active System Prices, at or above £190.00/MWh. The ten technologies shown match Figure 1; omitted technologies remain included in the tail and overall-share denominators.

What the figure measures

This separates two questions that the original conditional-outcome table combined: how frequently a technology is attributed marginal weight across all active-side periods, including extremes, and how much of the economically extreme price tail it represents. A value of zero represents proportional tail representation. The chart therefore measures concentration relative to each technology's overall marginal presence rather than ranking technologies by frequency or by their own conditional price percentile.

Main result. On the bid side, Wind is the most overrepresented technology in the lowest 5% of bid-active System Prices (12.2% overall versus 65.1% in the tail; +52.9 percentage points), while CCGT is the most underrepresented (-42.1 points). On the offer side, Pumped storage has the largest positive difference (18.5% overall versus 31.3% in the highest 5% of offer-active System Prices; +12.8 points), whereas Battery has the largest negative difference (-12.9 points).

Interpretation

Overall marginal frequency and extreme-price representation are not equivalent. Technologies to the right of zero are disproportionately associated with the price outcomes that are economically extreme for that regime; technologies to the left may still be common marginal candidates but account for a smaller share of those outcomes. This provides a sharper distinction than a simple technology ranking and complements Figure 2: the conditional intervals describe the price distribution when a technology is represented, whereas Figure 4 asks how attributed marginal weight is distributed within the system-wide directional tail.

Method and limitations

Each Settlement Period contributes one unit of weight divided equally among co-marginal BMUs. Overall shares use all valid periods within the relevant side; tail shares use the same weights only in periods beyond the pooled 2023–2025 side-specific threshold. Thresholds are inclusive, so price mass points can make the realised tail slightly larger than exactly 5%. The comparison is descriptive rather than causal, and pooled thresholds can reflect changes in the wider price environment across the study window. The complete table should be used for smaller technologies omitted from the main-text display.

Figure 5. Marginal technology composition across NIV direction and intensity

Figure 5. Marginal technology composition across NIV direction and intensity. Heatmap cells show each technology's tie-adjusted share of attributed marginal Settlement Period weight within each NIV bin. The seven principal technologies are displayed; visible shares may therefore sum to less than 100%, as omitted technologies remain included in each denominator. Column headers report median System Price and the number of valid Settlement Periods. NIV is measured in MWh per Settlement Period. The outer bins contain fewer than 300 periods and should be interpreted cautiously.

What the figure measures

Figures 1–3 distinguish long from short systems, but Figure 5 tests whether the attributed marginal mix also changes with the severity of imbalance. The bins are symmetric around zero: increasingly negative NIV represents progressively stronger long-system conditions, while increasingly positive NIV represents progressively stronger short-system conditions. The price values embedded in the headers link this physical condition to the observed central System Price without introducing a second visual scale or implying that NIV or the marginal technology alone caused the price outcome.

Main result. Technology composition varies within both regimes rather than changing only at the zero-NIV boundary. Battery's largest displayed share is 25.4% in the > 1,000 MWh bin; CCGT peaks at 48.8% in the −250 to 0 MWh bin. Wind reaches its highest share under < −1,000 MWh conditions, while pumped storage reaches its highest share under 500 to 1,000 MWh conditions. Across the two bins adjacent to zero NIV, median System Price rises from £61/MWh on the long side to £110/MWh on the short side—a conditional difference of £49/MWh, not an estimated causal effect of crossing the boundary. Across the full ordered range, the median rises monotonically from £-25/MWh to £128/MWh.

Interpretation

The binary active-side split is therefore necessary but incomplete. Technologies occupy different positions not only on either side of zero NIV but across the intensity distribution within each side. Reading the heatmap cells together with their column headers shows where changes in attributed marginal identity coincide with changes in the typical System Price. These are conditional descriptive patterns; they do not isolate technology effects from demand, renewable output, scarcity, actions taken outside the energy stack, or other contemporaneous market conditions.

Method and limitations

Each valid Settlement Period contributes a total marginal weight of one, divided equally among tied marginal BMUs and then aggregated by technology within its NIV bin. The outer thresholds are ±1,000 MWh rather than ±2,000 MWh because the observed 2023–2025 sample contains virtually no Settlement Periods beyond ±2,000 MWh; the selected symmetric bins retain meaningful tail samples while preserving a centred long-to-short comparison. The seven displayed rows do not sum to 100% where smaller technologies account for the remaining weight. Unequal bin counts are reported explicitly, and all results should be read as within-bin composition rather than frequency across the full sample.
